newsitem.title: USA: Chilean president renews push for NAFTA entry.
newsitem.headline: Chilean president renews push for NAFTA entry.

text.p: Chilean President Eduardo Frei, beginning a four-day visit to the United States, renewed his call on Monday for Chile's entry into the North American Free Trade Agreement.
"We reiterate Chile's interest in becoming part of this treaty," he said.

"Complete trade liberalization between Chile and the United States not only would strengthen our economic relations, but will also have a significant impact in the process of free trade in the Americas, which is an objective pursued by both countries," he added.

Frei said a majority of his countrymen believe in the concept of an open economy, and this year Chile will have achieved 14 years of sustained growth with the virtual doubling of per capita income in one decade.
"Economic freedom has yielded its fruits," he said, according to a translation of his prepared remarks released at a luncheon meeting where he spoke.
Chile was invited to join the North American trade bloc, which links the United States, Canada and Mexico, at the first Summit of the Americas in Miami in December, 1994.

But it has declined to go forward until President Clinton gets "fast track" authority from the U.S. Congress to negotiate trade accords. It fears special interest groups could too easily lobby Congress to derail trade pacts without the authority.
Trade between the United States and Chile passed the $6 billion mark last year, Frei said, with a $1.5 billion trade balance in favor of the United States.

The United States is one of the most important markets for Chilean salmon, wine and fresh fruit, while U.S. companies are among the chief foreign investors in Chile with billions of dollars invested, mainly in mining.
Frei, accompanied by 130 business people from his country, appeared at a lunch with regional U.S. business leaders. He is scheduled to meet later this week with Clinton and address Congress.

During Monday's appearance in Chicago he witnessed the signing of an agreement between CMS Energy Corp. of Dearborn, Mich., and Chile's Empresa Nacional de Electricidad S.A. to develop the $900 million Atacama pipeline and power project linking Argentina and Chile.

The agreement calls for construction of a natural gas pipeline that would run from the gas producing fields of northern Argentina to Mejillones in Chile, as well as a 600-megawatt gas-fueled power plant and a 10 million gallon (37.8 million litres) per-day water desalinization plant, both at Mejillones.

Victor Fryling, president of CMS, said the project "will significantly reduce electricity prices in northern Chile, saving the Chilean copper industry an estimated $40 million annually and promote competition between natural gas and other fuels."
